spans.text: This book started with a question I kept hearing from kids I know:
How do I actually make money online?
Not
“how do I become an influencer”
or
“how do I get famous.”
Just: how do I make something worth buying, find people who want it, and get paid for it, before I’m old enough to hold a traditional job?

The answer is more accessible than most adults realize. The internet has removed almost every barrier that used to keep young people out of business: you don’t need a storefront, inventory, startup capital, or years of experience. You need a skill, even a modest one, and the patience to turn it into something someone else will pay for.
That’s what this book teaches.

It doesn’t teach shortcuts. Every chapter is honest about the time and effort required. But it insists, with specific evidence and real examples, that starting is within reach right now, this week, with tools you can download for free today.
WHO THIS BOOK IS FOR

This book is for anyone between the ages of ten and fourteen who wants to start earning money online. You don’t need prior business experience, artistic talent, coding skills, or a big social media following. Every chapter starts from zero and walks you through a complete earning path, from first idea to first sale.
If you’re older or younger than the target age range and this book found you anyway, that’s fine. The skills here don’t expire.
HOW TO USE THIS BOOK

Each chapter introduces a named character who faces a real challenge and solves it in a way you can replicate. Read their story, then do the TRY THIS exercise at the end of the chapter. The exercise is the point: the knowledge only becomes useful when you apply it.

You don’t have to read every chapter before you start. If you already know which earning path interests you, skip directly to that chapter. If you’re not sure, start with Chapters 1 through 4 to build your foundation, then pick the Part Two chapter that sounds most like something you’d actually do.

The appendix includes a glossary of terms used throughout the book, platform age requirements, tax basics, and a guide for parents and educators. If you hit a word you don’t recognize, check the glossary first.
ABOUT THE KIDS FUTURE FUND

A portion of proceeds from this book supports the KIDS Future Fund, a program dedicated to helping children build long-term financial security through early investing and financial literacy. Chapter 1 covers the KFF mission in full. For more, visit kidsfuturefund.org.
Now let’s get started.
— Jeffrey Carrier

On a Saturday in March, Maya drew twelve cats. Not regular cats: cats with tiny crowns, cats in raincoats, cats giving a thumbs-up. She packaged them into a digital sticker set, uploaded the file to a free platform called Gumroad, priced it at $4, and sent the link to three friends.
By Sunday night, eleven strangers had bought it. She’d made $44.
Maya had been drawing her whole life. This was the first time anyone had paid her for it.

She didn’t rent a store. She didn’t ship anything. She didn’t need a business license or startup money or a parent’s credit card. She made her stickers on a tablet she already owned, using a free app she’d downloaded six months earlier just to doodle. She sold them while she was asleep.
That’s what this book is about.

Not a get-rich-quick scheme. Not a simplified version of adult business advice. A real, practical guide to something a lot of kids your age are already doing, making things online and getting paid for them.
WHAT MAKES A SIDE HUSTLE JUNIOR?
A Side Hustle Junior is a young person who creates something valuable and offers it to the world, usually online, often for money, always on their own terms.
That definition matters. Look at what it doesn’t say.

It doesn’t say you need to be a tech expert. It doesn’t say you need money to invest. It doesn’t say your parents need to set up an LLC (Limited Liability Corporation) or fill out forms. It says you need to create something valuable and offer it.

You already create things. Maybe you draw. Maybe you write stories or jokes. Maybe you build elaborate worlds in Minecraft and know instinctively how the game mechanics work in ways other kids don’t. Maybe you’re the person in your friend group who explains things clearly, who everyone asks for help on a subject they struggle with. Maybe you film things on your phone, make music, design things, take photos, or code games for fun.
Whatever your version of creating is, it counts. The internet turns it into an opportunity.
The
“online”

part is what changes the equation. The internet removes geography. A kid in one city can sell a digital illustration to a buyer in a different country. A twelve-year-old can publish an ebook that gets downloaded by adults who needed exactly that resource. A Scratch game made by a ten-year-old can be played by thousands of people.

The internet also removes inventory. When you sell a digital file, it never runs out. Maya could sell her sticker set to ten people or ten thousand: the file is identical, the cost to her is zero beyond the time she spent making it. That’s a different kind of business than anything that existed before the internet.
THE THREE WAYS TO EARN ONLINE
Every online income falls into one of three categories. Knowing which one you’re working in shapes everything about your strategy.

The first is selling a digital product. Maya’s sticker set is a digital product. So are ebooks, design templates, music tracks, Lightroom presets, fonts, printable worksheets, coding tutorials, and game mods. You create the thing once and sell it many times. Each sale requires no additional work from you: the platform handles the delivery automatically. This is the most scalable earning model available, and it’s accessible to young creators with no financial investment beyond their time and whatever free tools they’re already using.

The second is offering a service. This means using a skill you have to help someone accomplish something they can’t easily do themselves. Writing and editing. Designing logos and social media graphics. Building simple websites. Tutoring in a subject you’re strong in. Creating animations. Translating content. The difference between a service and a product is that a service trades your time directly for payment: you can’t sell the same hour twice. Services typically pay more per transaction than digital products, but they don’t scale the same way. You can raise your rates as you get better, take on more clients, or eventually turn a service into a product (a writing guide, a course, a template).

The third is building an audience and monetizing it. You create content consistently (YouTube videos, a blog, a podcast, a TikTok account) around something you genuinely love and know well. Over time, as people follow you, multiple income streams open up: ad revenue, sponsorships, affiliate commissions, and sales of your own products to an audience that already trusts you. This path is slower to pay off than the first two, but it compounds. An audience you’ve built over two years can generate income for a decade.

Most Side Hustle Juniors start with one path, usually digital products or services, and branch into the others over time. Maya started with digital products (sticker sets), added services (avatar commissions), and eventually added audience-building (a small Patreon membership). You don’t need to do all three at once. You need to pick one and actually start.
FIND YOUR NICHE
The three earning paths above describe how you’ll earn. Before you decide which path to start on, there’s an equally important question: what will you make?
The answer is your niche, the specific intersection of three things: what you’re good at, what you genuinely enjoy, and what other people actually want.
All three matter. Here’s why.

If you focus only on what you’re good at, you might produce technically strong work that nobody needs. If you focus only on what you enjoy, you might create things you love that the market doesn’t respond to. And if you focus only on what the market wants, without caring about the subject yourself, you’ll burn out and produce mediocre work.

The sweet spot is where all three overlap. Maya didn’t just draw cats because she could. She drew cats in a style that came naturally to her (skill), that she genuinely loved spending hours on (interest), and that turned out to have a ready market of digital planner users hunting for cute, expressive sticker packs (demand). That overlap is what made her first product a success, not luck, not timing, not a secret formula.
Finding your niche doesn’t have to be complicated. Ask yourself three questions and write down your answers:
What do I know how to do that others find hard or time-consuming? Think about skills people compliment you on, or things you finish quickly that seem to take others much longer.
What could I talk or write about for an hour without running out of material? Genuine enthusiasm shows in your work. It also makes the hard stretches easier to push through.

Is there evidence that people buy things in this area? A quick search on Gumroad, Etsy, or YouTube answers this fast. You’re not looking for zero competition: you’re looking for proof that a market exists. If similar products have reviews, sales badges, or active channels, that’s confirmation.
Write your three answers down. The place where they overlap is where your first product should live.
THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN DIGITAL AND PHYSICAL

Before the internet, selling something as a kid meant making it physically, carrying it somewhere, and finding buyers face to face. Lemonade stands. Baked goods. Handmade bracelets at school. Lawn mowing and car washing in the neighborhood.

That still works. It’s honest work and it builds real skills. But it has hard limits. You can only sell to people within walking distance. You run out of product. You have to show up in person every time.
Digital breaks all three of those limits.

When you sell a digital product, geography disappears. Your buyer can be anywhere. When you upload a sticker set, it’s simultaneously available to anyone with an internet connection: millions of potential customers, not the twelve households on your street.

The inventory limit disappears too. Physical goods run out. Digital files don’t. The same file can be downloaded by one buyer or one million buyers. The first thousand sales of Maya’s sticker set cost her exactly as much time as the first sale: the four hours she spent drawing the cats on a Saturday.
This is called scalability. When your earning isn’t limited by how many hours you have or how much physical product you can produce, you’ve entered a different category of income entirely.

The downside of digital is that it requires consistent effort in different ways, learning new tools, building an audience, iterating on your products. Nothing about this is passive in the beginning. But the ceiling is genuinely different from what physical selling allows, and that ceiling is accessible to you right now.
WHAT YOU ACTUALLY NEED
Here is the complete list of things you actually need to start:
A device: a computer, tablet, or even a phone. Anything that connects to the internet and runs the free tools covered in this book.
An internet connection: you almost certainly already have this.

A skill or interest you can make something from: drawing, writing, coding, explaining, designing, photographing, organizing. If you can’t immediately think of what yours is, that’s what the early chapters of this book are for.

Time: this is real. Building anything worthwhile takes hours. Not thousands of hours before you can start (Maya made her first $44 in about six hours of total work), but consistent time, applied regularly over weeks and months.

Here is what you don’t need: money to invest, a business license, a large social media following, expensive software, a course that costs $300, your parents to set up accounts for you, or anyone’s permission.

The tools in this field are mostly free. Canva, Gumroad, Scratch, Google Docs, Google Sites. All free. The platforms that charge do so only when you make a sale, meaning they take a percentage of money you’ve already earned. The knowledge is free, much of it is in this book, and the rest is a search query away.

What separates Side Hustle Juniors who build something real from those who stay in the planning phase is simple: they start. They make the first version of something, imperfect, small, not their best work, and they put it out. They learn from what happens. They make a second version. And they keep going.
THE KIDS FUTURE FUND MISSION

This book is part of the KIDS Future Fund, a program built on a single conviction: young people who learn to create economic value for themselves grow into adults who can build economic value for others.

The KIDS Future Fund exists to make sure that access to business knowledge isn’t limited by geography, income, or school curriculum. Most kids don’t learn how money works, how to build something, or how to earn independently, not because they’re not capable, but because nobody taught them. That’s the gap this program addresses.

A portion of the proceeds from this book go directly to the KIDS Future Fund. This book teaches you how to earn. The KFF is about what you do with what you earn — how to invest it, grow it, and build financial security over time. For more information, visit kidsfuturefund.org.

That’s bigger than pocket money. It’s about what happens to a kid who spends two years building things online, who ships products, handles money, receives feedback, solves problems, learns new tools, and figures out how to reach an audience. That kid graduates from school with a set of practical skills most adults don’t have. More importantly, they have a self-concept that’s different: they know they can make something from nothing. They’ve proved it.
WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND THE MONEY
Here is something adults rarely say out loud: most of what you’ll learn building an online income isn’t about money. The money is real and it matters, but it’s a byproduct of something larger.

When you build a product and put it up for sale, you are doing something most people, including most adults, have never done. You are making something, pricing it, and asking a stranger to decide whether it’s worth buying. That process teaches you more about how the world actually works than almost anything you’ll do in school.

You learn that feedback, even harsh feedback, is information. That a product that doesn’t sell isn’t a failure: it’s data about what needs to change. You learn how to revise, relaunch, and try again. You learn that the gap between an idea and a finished thing is crossed by sitting down and doing the work, not by waiting for perfect conditions.

You also learn how money moves. How a platform takes a cut. How taxes work at a basic level. How to keep records simple enough that you can actually tell whether you’re profitable. These aren’t adult problems: they’re life problems, and the earlier you understand them, the more control you have.

The KIDS Future Fund framework treats entrepreneurship as a form of literacy. Financial literacy. Creative literacy. The ability to read what the market wants and respond to it. These skills compound over time in the same way money compounds in a savings account. Every project you launch, even the ones that don’t work, adds to a base of experience that makes the next one more likely to succeed.

Think about where you’ll be in three years if you start building something today. Not theoretically. Specifically. If you spend 20 minutes a day on a digital project and launch something small every few months, you’ll have iterated through six to ten different products and services by the time you’re in high school. You’ll have handled real money. Received real feedback from real strangers. Figured out how to market something without a budget. Built a portfolio that shows what you can do, not just what you say you can do.
Most people your age will not do this. Not because they’re less capable, but because no one showed them it was possible and gave them the specific steps to try. That’s what this book is for.

The goal of this book isn’t to make you rich. The goal is to give you the tools, the framework, and the specific step-by-step guidance to start, and to show you that starting is within reach right now.
Everything after the first start is just iteration.
TRY THIS

1. Write down one thing you know how to do that others would find useful or enjoyable. It doesn’t have to be impressive: drawing simple animals, explaining fractions, writing funny captions, building things in Minecraft, taking photos. Write the first thing that comes to mind.
2. Search that thing on Gumroad or Etsy. Type
“[your skill] digital download”

into the search bar and look at what people are already selling. Don’t worry if it feels saturated: that means there’s a proven market. Note the price range. Note what the most popular listings look like.

3. Ask yourself honestly: could I make one of those? Not something perfect. A first version: the simplest, smallest possible version. If the answer is yes, or even maybe, you already have what you need to begin.
Maya stared at her Gumroad dashboard. $44. Real money, in a real account, from eleven people she’d never met.
Her first instinct was to spend it. There was a drawing app she’d been watching on sale for $19.99. And a stylus she’d bookmarked for months.
She bought both. That left $4.02.

Two weeks later, she had an idea for a second sticker pack. Bigger this time, more detailed, something she could sell for $8. She started designing. Then she hit a problem: the free version of her design tool put a watermark on exported files. To remove it, she needed to upgrade to the monthly plan: $9.99.
She had $4.02.
Maya had just learned the most important lesson in digital entrepreneurship: earning money is only the first step. What you do with it determines whether you keep earning.
THE THREE THINGS YOU DO WITH MONEY
Every dollar you receive does one of three things: it gets spent, it gets saved, or it gets reinvested back into your work.

Spending means using money for things you want or need right now: a treat, a game, something you’ve had your eye on. There’s nothing wrong with spending. It’s what money is for, in part. The problem is when spending is the only thing you do with money the moment it arrives.

Saving means setting money aside for a future goal. Maybe that’s a better device, a piece of software, a course that teaches you something marketable, or just a financial cushion for slower months. Savings give you options later. When you have no savings, every unexpected cost is a crisis.

Reinvesting means putting money back into your ability to earn: better tools, a platform upgrade, a professional template that helps your work look more credible, a course that expands your skill set. In business, this is called reinvesting in the operation. It’s how small, scrappy projects grow into something more significant over time.

Most beginners spend everything and then wonder why their work isn’t growing. The Side Hustle Juniors who scale have usually made one simple decision: they decide how to split their money before it arrives, not after.

A starting split that works for most young creators: 50% for spending on whatever you want, 30% for saving toward a specific goal, 20% for reinvesting in your work. The exact percentages matter less than having percentages at all. A plan, however rough, beats improvisation every time.
BUILD A SIMPLE BUDGET

A budget is a plan for money. It tells you where money is coming from, where it’s going, and whether those two things add up. It doesn’t have to be complicated. A budget can be three columns on a piece of paper or a five-tab spreadsheet, whatever you’ll actually use.
What matters is that it exists and that you look at it regularly.
Here’s what a simple creator budget looks like in practice:
STICKER BUSINESS — WEEK 1 BUDGET
INCOME
Gumroad sales this week: $44.00
Platform fees (Gumroad cut, ~10%): -$4.40
Net income: $39.60
SPLIT PLAN
Spend (50% of net): $19.80
Save (30% of net): $11.88
Reinvest (20% of net): $7.92
ACTUAL ALLOCATION
Drawing app: $19.99 (reinvest, tool)
Stylus: $19.99 (spend, want item)
Total spent/reinvested: $39.98
Remaining: -$0.38
Result: $0.38 over budget. Savings: $0.

When you write it out, the math is obvious. Maya’s problem wasn’t that she earned too little. She earned $39.60 net in a weekend. Her problem was that she didn’t separate her reinvestment purchases from her personal spending: she bought both items before checking whether the split held. A one-dollar mistake became a situation where she couldn’t pay for the next tool she needed.
The budget doesn’t restrict you. It shows you the choices before you make them instead of after.
HOW TO TRACK YOUR EARNINGS
Tracking means keeping a written record of every sale: when it happened, what sold, how much came in, what the platform took, and what you spent to make it. Not just the total: the details.
This matters for three concrete reasons.

First, tracking shows you what works. If you notice that your cat sticker set outsells your dog sticker set five to one, that’s information. You make more cat stickers. You can’t see those patterns without records.
“I think the cat ones do better”
is a feeling.
“My cat set has sold 47 units in three weeks, my dog set has sold 9”
is a fact you can act on.

Second, tracking shows you whether you’re actually profitable. Revenue, the money coming in, is not the same as profit. If you sell $100 worth of work in a month but spent $60 on tools and platform fees, your profit is $40. If you spent $110, you lost money this month even though you had sales. Profit is what’s left after all costs. You can’t calculate it without records.

Third, tracking builds a habit that compounds. People who know their numbers make better decisions consistently. People who wing it feel perpetually uncertain about whether things are going well or not. The habit of tracking, which takes maybe five minutes a week, is one of the highest-leverage things you can do for your business.

For now, a notes app or a piece of paper is enough. Log the date, what sold, gross revenue, platform fees deducted, and any costs you incurred. That’s your financial record. You can get more sophisticated as things grow.
UNDERSTAND REVENUE VERSUS PROFIT
Revenue is the total money that comes in before anything is subtracted. Profit is what’s left after you subtract all your costs.

A platform like Gumroad takes approximately 10% of each sale. Etsy takes a $0.20 listing fee per item plus a 6.5% transaction fee plus a payment processing fee. If you’re selling a $5 product on Etsy, you might actually receive about $3.90 after fees. That’s your real revenue per sale.

If you’re also paying $10/month for a design tool subscription, that cost comes out of your earnings too. If you sell ten items in a month at $5 each, you’ve grossed $50 in revenue, but after Etsy fees you might net $39, and after the software subscription you net $29. That’s your actual profit.

Knowing this matters for pricing. If you price your sticker set at $1 because it feels more accessible, and the platform keeps $0.40, you’re earning $0.60 per sale. A tool subscription at $10/month means you need to sell more than 16 sticker sets just to break even. At that point, your time isn’t being valued at all.
Price your work above your costs. Always know your costs first.
UNDERSTAND YOUR COSTS
Digital work feels free because you don’t buy raw materials. No canvas, no yarn, no wood. But costs exist: they’re just less visible.
Platform fees: every selling platform takes a cut. Know the percentage before you set your price, not after.

Tool subscriptions: design software, video editing apps, website hosting, premium fonts. These often run $5–$20 per month per tool. One subscription is manageable. Four subscriptions before you’ve made your first sale is a problem.
One-time purchases: a font license, a stock photo pack, a course. These hit once and can be worth it, but they come out of your budget.

Time: this isn’t a dollar cost, but it’s real. If you spend ten hours making something that earns $2, your hourly rate is $0.20. That might be fine when you’re learning and the experience is the point. It’s worth knowing either way.

When you price your product, start by adding up all costs, both the fixed monthly costs and the per-sale costs, then set a price that covers them and still leaves you a margin you feel good about. Most beginners underprice significantly. A digital sticker set that took four hours to design and delivers genuine creative value to buyers is worth more than $1.
THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN SPENDING AND INVESTING

Buying that $19.99 drawing app wasn’t a mistake in principle. A better tool that helps you produce higher-quality work faster is genuinely worth paying for. The mistake was making the purchase without checking whether it fit the budget and leaving nothing for savings.

An investment in your business is money spent on something that increases your ability to earn. A better drawing app: investment. A course that teaches you Etsy SEO (Search Engine Optimization is the process of improving a website to increase its visibility in organic search results): investment. A premium Canva subscription that unlocks templates your free account can’t access: potentially an investment, if you’re actively using Canva to make products.

Personal spending is money spent on something you want for yourself right now. Both are legitimate uses of money. The distinction isn’t about judging one as good and one as bad: it’s about knowing which one you’re doing in the moment of the decision.

Before any purchase, ask two questions: Does this increase my ability to earn, or is it something I want personally? And: does it fit my budget right now, or does buying it leave me unable to cover something I’ll need next?
Answering honestly, before you spend, keeps you in control of where things go.
SET A SAVINGS GOAL
Savings with no target feel pointless. Savings with a specific goal feel purposeful.
Pick something concrete. A better stylus: $40. A premium design tool subscription for three months: $30. A course on illustration: $50. A ring light for a video setup: $25.

Write the goal down. Write the dollar amount. Every time you receive money, put your 30% (or whatever percentage you’ve chosen) into a separate place, a second envelope, a separate bank account, a specific folder in a budgeting app, until you reach the goal.
When you hit it, you buy the thing. Not because you impulsively decided you wanted it today, but because you planned for it and earned it intentionally.

This feels slow at first. It is slow at first. But it becomes fast, much faster than the alternative, which is spending everything as it arrives and never having enough for the things that actually matter for your growth.
WHAT ABOUT TAXES?
This comes up eventually, so it’s worth addressing now.

In the United States, any self-employment income over $400 in a calendar year is reportable to the IRS, regardless of your age. If you earn $500 from Gumroad sales, that $500 is income that technically belongs on a tax return.

This sounds alarming. In practice, for most young entrepreneurs earning relatively small amounts, the tax owed is small or zero once deductions are applied: your tool expenses, platform fees, and other legitimate business costs reduce your taxable income. But the reporting obligation is real.

The important thing: keep records from the beginning. Every sale, every platform payout, every business expense. A simple spreadsheet or notebook log is enough. At the end of the year, if your earnings are meaningful, have a conversation with your parent and consult a tax professional if needed.
Several selling platforms send annual earnings summaries that simplify this process. Amazon KDP, Etsy, and Gumroad all provide year-end earnings reports you can use for tax preparation.

For most young creators just starting out, the earnings are small enough that taxes are minimal. But building the record-keeping habit now means you won’t have to reconstruct six months of sales history when it becomes necessary later.
A SECOND BUDGET SCENARIO
Maya’s first sticker pack sold $44 in one weekend. But what about a more common scenario, slower, steadier growth over a few months?
Here’s a more realistic example:
MONTH 3 — DIGITAL ART BUSINESS
MONTHLY INCOME
Sticker set sales (18 units × $4 net per sale): $72.00
Avatar commissions (2 completed × $20): $40.00
Total income: $112.00
MONTHLY COSTS
Canva Pro subscription: $13.00
Procreate (one-time purchase, already paid: $0 this month)
Etsy listing fees (8 listings × $0.20): $1.60
Transaction fees (estimated): ~$7.00
Total costs: $21.60
NET PROFIT: $90.40
Spend ($45.20): personal spending this month
Save ($27.12): toward tablet upgrade fund
Reinvest ($18.08): toward a font license for ebook covers
SAVINGS ACCOUNT TOTAL: $62.48 (after three months)

$90 net profit in month three, from part-time creative work alongside school. Not life-changing money yet, but $62 in savings toward something specific, and growing monthly. By month six, if sales hold, that’s over $120 in savings accumulated from work that keeps paying without requiring new effort each month.
The compounding doesn’t start feeling significant right away. It starts feeling significant when you look back six months and realize how far it’s moved from where it started.
TRY THIS

1. Write down the three categories: Spend, Save, Reinvest. Assign a percentage to each. If you have no idea where to start, use this as a default: 10% Spend, 30% Save, 60% Reinvest. Adjust from there based on what you’re saving toward and what your business actually needs. Write your split before you earn anything. The point is to decide in advance, not in the moment.
2. Find out the exact fee structure of one platform you plan to sell on. Calculate: if you sold a product for $8, how much would you actually keep after fees?

3. List any tools or subscriptions you’re currently using or want to use for your business. Add up the monthly cost. That number is your break-even point: how much you need to earn each month before you’re actually making money. Know this number before you launch.
